title: But?
theme: Faith that remains with God through pain, questions, and uncertainty without making understanding a condition for following Him.
opening: Maybe faith is not having no questions. Maybe it is refusing to make the answers a condition for staying.
prayer: Prayer  Lord, I do not always understand Your ways, and sometimes what I cannot understand hurts deeply. Keep me from turning my faith into a bargain with You. Let me bring You my questions, anger, grief and confusion without allowing them to become conditions for loving You. When I find myself saying, “I will follow You, but…,” give me the courage to release whatever comes next. I do not need to understand everything You are doing to remain with You. Help me stay. Amen.
body:
What stayed with me in today’s reading was Job’s persistence. He is suffering. He doesn’t understand what has happened to him, and he certainly doesn’t pretend that he does. He knows how small his understanding is compared with God’s: “Should he come near me, I see him not; should he pass by, I am not aware of him.”

There is something almost painful about that. Job wants God. He wants answers from God. He is hurting before God. But he does not make his pain a condition for remaining with God.

There is no but.

That struck me when I read today’s Gospel because suddenly there are buts everywhere.

“I will follow you wherever you go.” But there will be no comfortable place to rest.

“Follow me.” But first let me bury my father.

“I will follow you, Lord.” But first let me say farewell.

Jesus’ responses sound severe, but maybe He is exposing something we do constantly. We want to follow Him, but we also want to determine the conditions under which we will follow.

I trust You, but I need to understand this.

I will follow You, but first I need to fix what is happening in my life.

I believe You are with me, but why did You let this happen?

Job asks why too. That matters to me because I don’t think faith requires us to stop questioning. Job grieves, argues, pleads and struggles. His suffering is real, and he does not hide any of it from God.

But he stays.

Maybe that is the difference.

Pain is not the but. Questions are not the but. Anger, grief and confusion do not necessarily separate us from God. The but appears when we make something a condition of remaining with Him.

I will trust You if…

I will follow You when…

I will believe You as long as…

How easily those conditions enter our faith.

Job eventually receives restoration, but I don’t think the point is that he remained faithful and therefore God gave everything back. That would make faith another bargain: I will trust You so that You will restore what I have lost.

Something deeper happens to Job. Before his circumstances are restored, he encounters God. He discovers the limits of his own understanding and remains in relationship with the One whose ways he cannot possibly comprehend.

There is something freeing about admitting that.

We are human. We see such a small part of what God sees, yet we continually try to fit His ways inside our understanding. When they don’t fit, we struggle. I certainly do.

Maybe I don’t need to understand everything in order to remain close to Him.

I can hurt and stay.

I can question and stay.

I can tell God that I don’t understand what He is doing and stay.

I can even ask Him why.

Faith does not require me to pretend that suffering doesn’t hurt. It asks something harder of me: not to make the ending of that suffering the price God must pay for my trust.

Job did not know where his story was going while he was living it. Neither do we.

Maybe sometimes the most honest prayer we can offer is also the simplest:

I don’t understand.

I am hurting.

I am still here.

And so are You.
